## Overview

The Safwa are an ethnic and linguistic group based in the mountains of the Mbeya Region, Tanzania. The source says that the Safwa people were moved to Mbeya Tanzania from Zambia. Safwa belongs to the large Niger–Congo language family group and is also known as Ishisafwa, Cisafwa, or Kisafwa. Its dialects are Guruka, Mbwila, Poroto, and Songwe. The Safwa were conquered by the Wasangu in 1893 and were divided into many small chiefdoms. They were described as loosely organized and close to stateless, while equality remained central to their identity and ideology. Their population was estimated at approximately 158,000 in 1957 and expected to exceed 450,000 after the 2012 national census.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Men’s weaving** — Weaving by men was a normal occupation. By 1909, however, a man could earn four times more cloth through wages than by weaving it himself, and the weaving industry began to decline after the importation of European cloth.

### Clothing & dress

 They state only that men’s weaving was a normal occupation and that European cloth contributed to the decline of the weaving industry. The sources also record that chiefs could not shave their heads, although they could cut their hair, because they were responsible for good rain.

### Architecture

The sources describe villages that had fences against enemies and wild animals. Close to the fence, each village had a shelter or lodge where mature men sat together and where travelers and older youths ate and slept. Maintaining this structure was considered a community obligation. They also state that Safwa settlements were not historically concentrated: the Safwas had not previously lived in concentrated settlements and disliked them.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 They mention livestock and agricultural products in connection with cleansing rites following the birth of twins.

### Jewelry & body adornment

 They state that after the death of a chief, all men, women, and children shaved their heads, while chiefs themselves were not permitted to shave their heads.

## Music & performance

 They state that the Wasafwa were communal hunters and that hunting songs and dances were performed after the hunters had been inoculated against witchcraft. The people then waited for the successful return of the hunters and for the meat to be distributed.

The sources also describe children in the 1890s playing at assaulting fortresses. This is recorded as children’s play rather than as a named dramatic or musical form. No wedding music, funeral music, court performance, instrumental tradition, or named song repertoire is identified.

## Dance & theatre

The sources mention dances performed by communal hunters after inoculation against witchcraft. These dances accompanied hunting songs and occurred in anticipation of the hunters’ return and the distribution of meat. No named Safwa dance, theatre form, mask tradition, shadow-puppet tradition, or distinction between ceremonial and entertainment performance is provided.

The account of children playing at assaulting fortresses in the 1890s is the only other performance-like activity described.

## Festivals & rituals

 They do describe several life-cycle and ritual practices.

Following birth, a child began to be force-fed two to three days later with millet mush. The child was laid on its back, the mush was placed in its mouth, and the mother continued pushing it beyond nutritional needs. The sources state that this was thought to prepare the child for a later life of feast or famine.

The birth of twins was described as a severe shock. Parents normally allowed one twin to die of hunger because of fear concerning two angry spirits. A complex cleansing of the village and parents was then carried out by a “medicine doctor,” requiring livestock and agricultural products. The process could take two years, or ten years if both twins lived, before the twins were treated as regular members of the community. The sources state that children handicapped at birth were said to be treated as normal children and that albino children were said not to be put to death.

The death of a chief involved secretive succession practices. Counselors selected a successor, usually a son or grandson, and the choice was concealed. The body was buried while people slept; afterward, men, women, and children shaved their heads, women brewed beer, and a new chief was brought out only after a month.

## Foodways

The sources name millet mush, livestock, agricultural products, beer, corn, beans, vegetables, and meat. Two to three days after birth, a child was force-fed millet mush. Following the birth of twins, livestock and agricultural products were required for cleansing rites. After the death of a chief, women quickly brewed beer.

Safwa chiefs were subject to particular dietary restrictions. Some avoided dog meat, lions, elephants, rhinoceros, and hippopotamus. The sources explain these restrictions in symbolic terms: dogs were said to cause the stomach to bark, while lions, elephants, and rhinoceros were rulers of the wild, and hippopotamuses were associated with spots on the skin. Some chiefs could not eat corn and beans cooked together or the leaves of vegetables because this would mark them as poor.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources state that the Safwa apparently had no traditional history. They do, however, mention hunting songs and dances and describe children’s play involving assaults on fortresses in the 1890s.

The sources identify several Safwa poets and writers: Christopher Mwashinga, Castro D.Shazeha, Narwimba, and Imani Mwilizi. Christopher Mwashinga is specifically identified as an author. No titles, genres, literary institutions, or preservation projects are supplied.

## Language & religion

Safwa, also called Kisawfa, is a Bantu language spoken by the Safwa people of the Mbeya Region of Tanzania. It belongs to the Niger–Congo language family. The dialects named by the sources are Guruka, Mbwila, Poroto, and Songwe. The ISO 639-3 language code is sbk. The sources describe uncertainty over whether Kisafwa has a seven-vowel or five-vowel system and report differences in noun-class prefixes and vocabulary among varieties.

Originally, the Safwas were traditionalists who worshiped ancestors. Elders or priests visited a sacred grove during disasters such as lack of rain or outbreaks of killer diseases. They gave gifts to ancestors and prayed for rain or the removal of diseases. A sacred grove at Iganjo in Igawilo is described as approximately 15 kilometers from Mbeya city center.

In recent decades, many Safwas have accepted Christianity or Islam. About 22% are reported to adhere to different Christian denominations, including the Assemblies of God, Roman Catholics, Seventh-day Adventists, Jehovah’s Witnesses, and Moravians. A large number, especially among older and not-so-old people, remain traditionalists.
